screens.title: Mastering Inheritance and Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll build a clear, practical understanding of inheritance and polymorphism in Java. You'll learn why we create subclasses with the extends keyword, how constructor chaining with super works, and how method overriding creates different behavior for objects at runtime. We will use the banking Account and SavingsAccount example to show constructor calls, and a shapes exercise to practice polymorphic arrays. You will also learn the safety rules for upcasting and downcasting, how to use instanceof as a guard, and why @Override protects you from accidental overloads. These ideas let you write reusable base classes, specialize behavior in subclasses, and treat diverse objects uniformly through common references. Knowing these patterns keeps code maintainable and reduces duplication. By the end of the lesson you will be able to explain an "is-a" relationship, implement an inheritance hierarchy, reason about which method runs at runtime, and apply safe casting checks. Consider how a single bank Account reference can represent many account types — that is the practical power you'll take away.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will meet four concrete objectives that work together. First, explain the core principles of inheritance and polymorphism so you can describe why subclasses share behavior and how an object can take many forms. For example, you will be able to explain how a SavingsAccount is an Account and what that implies for fields and methods. Second, implement inheritance using the extends keyword and correctly override methods; you will write subclass constructors that call super and use @Override to prevent accidental overloading. Third, differentiate between upcasting and downcasting. You will recognize that assigning a subclass instance to a superclass reference is always safe, while converting a superclass reference back into a subclass requires an explicit cast and an instanceof check to avoid runtime errors. Fourth, utilize the super keyword to invoke superclass constructors and methods and understand dynamic method dispatch so you can predict which method will run at runtime. These competencies let you design reusable hierarchies and write polymorphic code with confidence.

screens.title: What is Inheritance?
screens.narratorSegment: Inheritance is a foundational object-oriented mechanism that lets a new class acquire fields and methods from an existing class so you don't duplicate code. When class B extends class A, B becomes a subclass and A is the superclass. This creates an "is-a" relationship: a SavingsAccount is an Account. The subclass inherits public and protected members and can access them directly, while private members remain encapsulated and can only be used indirectly through superclass methods. A concrete example is a banking Account with accountNumber, balance, deposit, and withdraw. Instead of copying those fields into every account type, SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount extend Account and reuse its logic. That makes code easier to maintain: a bug fix in Account's deposit method benefits every subclass. A common misconception is thinking inheritance means copying code; it does not duplicate members physically, it reuses behavior through type relationships. Another subtle point: inheritance defines both behavior reuse and a type relationship. Use inheritance when the subclass truly is a specialized form of the superclass; prefer composition when you only need to reuse behavior without expressing an "is-a" relationship. Key takeaway: inheritance promotes reuse and establishes meaningful type hierarchies.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Inheritance lets a subclass reuse fields and methods from a superclass and models an "is-a" relationship.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is Inheritance?
An "is-a" relationship that enables subclasses to reuse fields and behavior from a superclass.
  • Subclass reuses public and protected members from its superclass.
  • Private members are not directly accessible but available via superclass methods.
  • Use inheritance when the relationship is truly "is-a" rather than just reuse.
Key Takeaway

Inheritance models type relationships and centralizes shared behavior to reduce duplication.

Example: Account → SavingsAccount
class Account {
  protected String accountNumber;
  protected double balance;
  // constructor, deposit, withdraw
}

class SavingsAccount extends Account {
  private double interestRate;
  public SavingsAccount(String accNo, double bal, double ir) {
    super(accNo, bal);
    this.interestRate = ir;
  }
  @Override
  public void withdraw(double amount) { /* specialized rules */ }
}
Analogy
Family tree
Subclass is a child that inherits traits from a parent class.
Common mistake
Using inheritance for code reuse only
Prefer composition when there is no true "is-a" relationship.

screens.title: Using extends and overriding methods
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through implementing a subclass that changes behavior. In the Account example, SavingsAccount extends Account to reuse fields and methods. The subclass constructor calls super with accountNumber and initialBalance to ensure the inherited fields are initialized correctly. Omitting that explicit super call can cause a compile error when the superclass lacks a default constructor. SavingsAccount also overrides withdraw to impose a transaction fee. Use the @Override annotation so the compiler confirms your signature matches an inherited method; otherwise you might create an overloaded method by mistake. A concrete walkthrough: define Account with protected balance and deposit/withdraw methods. Define SavingsAccount extending Account. In its constructor call super(accountNumber, initialBalance) and assign interestRate. Implement applyInterest by computing interest and calling deposit to reuse superclass logic. When you override withdraw, make sure to check the balance against amount plus fee. This pattern keeps shared logic in the superclass, while subclasses implement specific rules. A good test is to create a SavingsAccount, call deposit, applyInterest, and call withdraw to observe the specialized behavior. Using extends and overriding methods means use extends and super to reuse initialization, and @override to change inherited behavior safely.. In practical terms, implementing savingsaccount from account and changing behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Implement & Override
keyIdea.text: Use extends and super to reuse initialization, and @Override to change inherited behavior safely.

content.html:
Implementation
extends and @Override
Constructor chaining and method overriding demonstrate specialization.
class SavingsAccount extends Account {
  private double interestRate;

  public SavingsAccount(String accountNumber, double initialBalance, double interestRate) {
    super(accountNumber, initialBalance);
    this.interestRate = interestRate;
  }

  public void applyInterest() {
    double interest = balance * interestRate;
    deposit(interest);
  }

  @Override
  public void withdraw(double amount) {
    double fee = 0.50;
    if (amount > 0 && balance >= amount + fee) {
      balance -= (amount + fee);
    }
  }
}
Explanation bullets
  • super(...) invokes the superclass constructor to initialize inherited fields.
  • @Override signals to the compiler you intend to override, preventing signature mistakes.
  • Calling deposit from applyInterest reuses superclass code and respects encapsulation.
Scenario
Banking flow
Create SavingsAccount, call applyInterest, then withdraw and verify the fee applied.
Key Takeaway

Always match overridden method signatures and prefer @Override for safety.

screens.title: Constructor Chaining and super()
screens.narratorSegment: Constructor chaining determines how object state is initialized across a class hierarchy. When you instantiate a subclass, Java first ensures the superclass constructor runs so inherited fields are properly set. If the superclass has a no-argument constructor, Java inserts an implicit super call when you don't specify one. But if the superclass only defines constructors that require arguments, you must explicitly call super with the correct parameters; otherwise the compiler raises an error. For example, Account expects accountNumber and initialBalance. SavingsAccount's constructor must call super(accountNumber, initialBalance). This guarantees the inherited balance field is initialized before the subclass assigns its own fields. A misconception is that subclass fields initialize before the superclass; in reality the superclass constructor runs first. A simple test is to add logging or print statements in each constructor to observe the order. The practical takeaway: always match your superclass constructor requirements with explicit super calls to avoid compile-time issues and ensure consistent state. Constructor Chaining and super() means superclass constructors run first; use explicit super(...) when the superclass lacks a no-arg constructor.. In practical terms, how superclass initialization works and common errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Superclass constructors run first; use explicit super(...) when the superclass lacks a no-arg constructor.

content.html:
Process Flow
Constructor chaining
Superclass initialization always precedes subclass initialization.
  1. Call new Subclass(...) from code.
  2. Implicit or explicit call to superclass constructor occurs first.
  3. Superclass fields initialize, then subclass fields run its constructor body.
  4. If superclass has no no-arg constructor, explicit super(...) is required.
Example check
class Account {
  public Account(String id, double b) {
    System.out.println("Account constructor");
  }
}

class SavingsAccount extends Account {
  public SavingsAccount(String id, double b, double r) {
    super(id, b); // required
    System.out.println("SavingsAccount constructor");
  }
}
Pro tip
Add simple logging in constructors to verify initialization order while debugging hierarchies.

screens.title: Access Levels in Inheritance
screens.narratorSegment: Access modifiers define which members a subclass can see and reuse. Public members are visible everywhere and available to subclasses without restriction. Protected members are visible to subclasses and classes in the same package; they are often used to permit controlled access to important fields while still preventing public exposure. Private members are hidden inside the declaring class and cannot be accessed directly by subclasses; they can be used through public or protected accessor methods provided by the superclass. In the Account example, balance is declared protected so SavingsAccount can update it directly. A common misunderstanding is that private means inherited; it is not. Private members are present in the class but invisible to subclasses. When designing hierarchies, prefer private fields with protected or public accessor methods if you need tighter control over how subclasses modify state. This encapsulation preserves invariants and prevents fragile subclass implementations that break superclass assumptions. Access Levels in Inheritance means public: everywhere, protected: subclass + package, private: only inside declaring class; prefer controlled access over exposing internals.. In practical terms, public, protected, and private — what a subclass can use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison
Access Levels
public
Accessible from any class; safe for API methods you intend to expose.
protected
Accessible to subclasses and same-package classes — useful for intended extension points.
private
Hidden to subclasses; use accessors if subclasses must interact with internal state.
Example: balance field
Declare balance protected if subclasses should update it directly; prefer private with protected setters for stricter control.
Scenario
Refactoring
If subclasses misuse protected fields, refactor to private plus controlled methods to protect invariants.
Common mistake

Making many fields protected exposes internals and creates fragile subclass dependencies.

screens.title: Method Overriding and @Override
screens.narratorSegment: Method overriding is when a subclass provides a new implementation for a method already defined in its superclass. The runtime will call the subclass version when the actual object belongs to the subclass, even if the reference type is the superclass. The @Override annotation is an important safeguard: it tells the compiler you intend to override a method and causes a compile-time error if the signatures don't match, preventing accidental overloads. For example, SavingsAccount overrides withdraw to apply a fee. If you mistakenly change the parameter list, without @Override the compiler treats this as an overloaded method and the original withdraw will still be used when referenced through an Account type. A good practice is always to annotate intended overrides and run unit tests that exercise the polymorphic pathways. Also ensure that overriding methods preserve expected behavior or document deliberate changes to contracts like permitted side effects or exceptions. Overriding is a powerful tool when used to specialize behavior while preserving the superclass contract. Method Overriding and @Override means use @override to ensure the compiler enforces signature matching and avoid accidental method overloading.. In practical terms, when a subclass changes inherited behavior safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Override safely
keyIdea.text: Use @Override to ensure the compiler enforces signature matching and avoid accidental method overloading.

content.html:
Definition
Method Overriding
Provide a subclass implementation for a superclass method and ensure matching signatures.
Example
@Override
public void withdraw(double amount) {
  // specialized withdrawal logic
}
Why @Override matters
  • Detects mismatched signatures at compile time.
  • Prevents accidental creation of overloaded methods.
  • Improves readability by signaling intent to other developers.
Check
Run tests that call overridden methods through superclass references to ensure the subclass behavior executes.

screens.title: Dynamic Method Dispatch
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic method dispatch is the runtime mechanism that chooses which overridden method executes based on the actual object, not the reference type. This allows you to write code that operates on a superclass reference while getting subclass behavior when the object is a subclass. Consider Account myAccount = new SavingsAccount(...); when you call myAccount. withdraw(100), the JVM inspects the actual object referenced — SavingsAccount — and calls its withdraw method. This is what makes polymorphism practical: code that manipulates Account references can work uniformly with many specialized account types. A useful misconception check: compile-time type determines which methods the compiler permits you to call, but runtime type determines which implementation runs for overridden methods. So if a method exists only on SavingsAccount, calling it without a cast fails at compile time even if the object is a SavingsAccount at runtime. Dynamic dispatch supports extensibility: you can add new subclasses and the same code will work with their specific behavior automatically. A good design tip is to program to interfaces or abstract base classes so clients depend on stable contracts while implementations vary.

keyIdea.title: Runtime dispatch
keyIdea.text: The method implementation executed is chosen at runtime using the object's actual type, enabling polymorphic behavior.

content.html:
Runtime Behavior
Dynamic Method Dispatch
The JVM selects the overridden method implementation based on the object's runtime class.
Example call pattern for testing:
Account a = new SavingsAccount("S123", 1000, 0.02);
a.withdraw(100); // executes SavingsAccount.withdraw
Explanation
  • The compiler checks that withdraw exists on the reference type Account.
  • At runtime, the JVM dispatches to the overriding method on the actual object.
  • Adding subclasses does not require changing client code that uses the superclass.
Misconception
The reference type limits compile-time calls; the object type determines which overridden method runs.
Key Takeaway

Polymorphism via dynamic dispatch lets code work with general types while concrete types determine behavior at runtime.

screens.title: Upcasting and Downcasting
screens.narratorSegment: Upcasting and downcasting describe converting between reference types in inheritance hierarchies. Upcasting is implicit and safe: you can assign a subclass object to a superclass reference without a cast. For example, Account a = new SavingsAccount(...); is an upcast done automatically. Upcasting limits what you can call at compile time to members available on the superclass. Downcasting converts a superclass reference back to a subclass reference and requires an explicit cast, for example (SavingsAccount) a. This is potentially unsafe because if the referenced object is not actually a SavingsAccount you will get a ClassCastException. The best practice is to check the object's actual type first using instanceof before performing the cast. The chapter example demonstrates this pattern: if (generalAccount instanceof SavingsAccount) { SavingsAccount s = (SavingsAccount) generalAccount; s. applyInterest(); } Using instanceof ensures safety and allows access to subclass-only methods. A useful mental model: upcast to generalize behavior; downcast only when you need specialization and you've verified the object's type. Upcasting and Downcasting means upcast implicitly to generalize; downcast explicitly only after instanceof checks to avoid classcastexception.. In practical terms, when casts are implicit, when they are required, and how to stay safe. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them
screens.narratorSegment: Working with inheritance introduces several common pitfalls you should actively guard against. First, forgetting to call super in a subclass constructor is a frequent source of compile errors when the superclass lacks a default constructor. Always match the superclass constructor signature when needed. Second, accidental overloading happens when a subclass method looks like an override but its signature differs; without @Override the compiler won't warn you and your intended override won't run. Third, unsafe downcasts can produce ClassCastException at runtime; use instanceof checks to verify the object's actual type before casting. Another mistake is overexposing internal state by making many fields protected; this leads to fragile subclasses that depend on internal structure. Prefer private fields with well-defined protected or public accessors when appropriate. Finally, misunderstandings about dynamic dispatch can cause surprises: the compile-time reference type controls what you can call, while the runtime object type controls which overridden method is executed. A simple habit checklist—use @Override, call super properly, minimize protected fields, and guard downcasts—will reduce most issues. screens.title: Designing with Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism is most effective when you program to a stable abstraction — a superclass or interface — rather than concrete implementations. Design hierarchies where the superclass defines the contract that clients rely on, and subclasses implement variations. For example, an Account base can expose deposit, withdraw, and getBalance; clients depend only on these methods and can accept any account subtype. When adding new account types you won't need to change client code. Keep hierarchies shallow when possible: deep inheritance chains increase fragility and coupling. Prefer composition over inheritance when you need to reuse behavior but cannot honestly express an "is-a" relationship. Also document subclass contracts: what side effects or exceptions are permissible. Finally, use unit tests that exercise polymorphic behavior through base-class references; this catches mismatched overrides and behavioral regressions early. By combining clear contracts, limited inheritance depth, and disciplined testing, you keep polymorphism a tool for extensibility rather than a source of confusion. Designing with Polymorphism means program to abstractions, limit inheritance depth, prefer composition when appropriate, and test polymorphic paths.. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll build a clear, practical understanding of inheritance and polymorphism in Java. You'll learn why we create subclasses with the extends keyword, how constructor chaining with super works, and how method overriding creates different behavior for objects at runtime. We will use the banking Account and SavingsAccount example to show constructor calls, and a shapes exercise to practice polymorphic arrays. You will also learn the safety rules for upcasting and downcasting, how to use instanceof as a guard, and why @Override protects you from accidental overloads. These ideas let you write reusable base classes, specialize behavior in subclasses, and treat diverse objects uniformly through common references. Knowing these patterns keeps code maintainable and reduces duplication. By the end of the lesson you will be able to explain an "is-a" relationship, implement an inheritance hierarchy, reason about which method runs at runtime, and apply safe casting checks. Consider how a single bank Account reference can represent many account types — that is the practical power you'll take away.

By the end of this chapter you will meet four concrete objectives that work together. First, explain the core principles of inheritance and polymorphism so you can describe why subclasses share behavior and how an object can take many forms. For example, you will be able to explain how a SavingsAccount is an Account and what that implies for fields and methods. Second, implement inheritance using the extends keyword and correctly override methods; you will write subclass constructors that call super and use @Override to prevent accidental overloading. Third, differentiate between upcasting and downcasting. You will recognize that assigning a subclass instance to a superclass reference is always safe, while converting a superclass reference back into a subclass requires an explicit cast and an instanceof check to avoid runtime errors. Fourth, utilize the super keyword to invoke superclass constructors and methods and understand dynamic method dispatch so you can predict which method will run at runtime. These competencies let you design reusable hierarchies and write polymorphic code with confidence.

This second objectives slide drills into how you will practice the concepts. You will implement inheritance using extends by building classes that reuse fields and behavior rather than copying code. For constructor chaining you'll explicitly call super with parameters to initialize inherited state and observe what happens if you omit it. For polymorphism you will place subclass instances into arrays of the superclass type and iterate to observe which overridden method executes; this demonstrates dynamic method dispatch. For safe casting you will use instanceof before downcasting to access subclass-only methods and understand why failing to check leads to runtime exceptions. Each objective has a short verification step: write a SavingsAccount that overrides withdraw and shows a transaction fee; create a Shape hierarchy with Circle and Rectangle and iterate over a Shape[] calling calculateArea(); and perform a downcast guarded by instanceof to call applyInterest. Practicing these tasks verifies understanding and prevents common mistakes in real code.

Inheritance is a foundational object-oriented mechanism that lets a new class acquire fields and methods from an existing class so you don't duplicate code. When class B extends class A, B becomes a subclass and A is the superclass. This creates an "is-a" relationship: a SavingsAccount is an Account. The subclass inherits public and protected members and can access them directly, while private members remain encapsulated and can only be used indirectly through superclass methods. A concrete example is a banking Account with accountNumber, balance, deposit, and withdraw. Instead of copying those fields into every account type, SavingsAccount and CheckingAccount extend Account and reuse its logic. That makes code easier to maintain: a bug fix in Account's deposit method benefits every subclass. A common misconception is thinking inheritance means copying code; it does not duplicate members physically, it reuses behavior through type relationships. Another subtle point: inheritance defines both behavior reuse and a type relationship. Use inheritance when the subclass truly is a specialized form of the superclass; prefer composition when you only need to reuse behavior without expressing an "is-a" relationship. Key takeaway: inheritance promotes reuse and establishes meaningful type hierarchies.

Let's walk through implementing a subclass that changes behavior. In the Account example, SavingsAccount extends Account to reuse fields and methods. The subclass constructor calls super with accountNumber and initialBalance to ensure the inherited fields are initialized correctly. Omitting that explicit super call can cause a compile error when the superclass lacks a default constructor. SavingsAccount also overrides withdraw to impose a transaction fee. Use the @Override annotation so the compiler confirms your signature matches an inherited method; otherwise you might create an overloaded method by mistake. A concrete walkthrough: define Account with protected balance and deposit/withdraw methods. Define SavingsAccount extending Account. In its constructor call super(accountNumber, initialBalance) and assign interestRate. Implement applyInterest by computing interest and calling deposit to reuse superclass logic. When you override withdraw, make sure to check the balance against amount plus fee. This pattern keeps shared logic in the superclass, while subclasses implement specific rules. A good test is to create a SavingsAccount, call deposit, applyInterest, and call withdraw to observe the specialized behavior. Using extends and overriding methods means use extends and super to reuse initialization, and @override to change inherited behavior safely.. In practical terms, implementing savingsaccount from account and changing behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Constructor chaining determines how object state is initialized across a class hierarchy. When you instantiate a subclass, Java first ensures the superclass constructor runs so inherited fields are properly set. If the superclass has a no-argument constructor, Java inserts an implicit super call when you don't specify one. But if the superclass only defines constructors that require arguments, you must explicitly call super with the correct parameters; otherwise the compiler raises an error. For example, Account expects accountNumber and initialBalance. SavingsAccount's constructor must call super(accountNumber, initialBalance). This guarantees the inherited balance field is initialized before the subclass assigns its own fields. A misconception is that subclass fields initialize before the superclass; in reality the superclass constructor runs first. A simple test is to add logging or print statements in each constructor to observe the order. The practical takeaway: always match your superclass constructor requirements with explicit super calls to avoid compile-time issues and ensure consistent state. Access modifiers define which members a subclass can see and reuse. Public members are visible everywhere and available to subclasses without restriction. Protected members are visible to subclasses and classes in the same package; they are often used to permit controlled access to important fields while still preventing public exposure. Private members are hidden inside the declaring class and cannot be accessed directly by subclasses; they can be used through public or protected accessor methods provided by the superclass. For example, an Account base can expose deposit, withdraw, and getBalance; clients depend only on these methods and can accept any account subtype. When adding new account types you won't need to change client code. Keep hierarchies shallow when possible: deep inheritance chains increase fragility and coupling. Prefer composition over inheritance when you need to reuse behavior but cannot honestly express an "is-a" relationship. Also document subclass contracts: what side effects or exceptions are permissible. Finally, use unit tests that exercise polymorphic behavior through base-class references; this catches mismatched overrides and behavioral regressions early. By combining clear contracts, limited inheritance depth, and disciplined testing, you keep polymorphism a tool for extensibility rather than a source of confusion. Let's summarize the essential terms and their practical meaning. Inheritance is the mechanism that lets a subclass acquire fields and methods from a superclass and models an "is-a" relationship. The extends keyword declares that relationship and super is used to access the immediate parent's constructor or methods. Method overriding lets subclasses provide specialized behavior; annotate intended overrides with @Override so the compiler checks your intent. Polymorphism and dynamic method dispatch mean that the JVM chooses which overridden method to run based on the object's runtime type, allowing code written against a superclass to operate on many concrete types. Upcasting is implicit and safe when assigning a subclass instance to a superclass reference; downcasting requires an explicit cast and should be guarded by instanceof to avoid ClassCastException. Keep interfaces and base classes stable, prefer composition when appropriate, and test polymorphic pathways. These ideas together let you write reusable, extensible, and safer object-oriented code.

A final quick reference to keep nearby while you code. First: use extends to express an "is-a" relationship and call super in subclass constructors when the superclass requires parameters. Second: always annotate intended overrides with @Override; this prevents signature mismatches and accidental overloading. Third: upcast to generalize and only downcast after confirming the object's type with instanceof to avoid ClassCastException. These three habits — explicit constructor chaining, consistent use of @Override, and guarded downcasts — catch the majority of common mistakes with inheritance and polymorphism. When you combine them with clear base-class contracts and focused unit tests, your hierarchies remain understandable and robust.
